name: Question 10
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/e8d2665ab162ff21e358a80a6e42659b0385244a08d94f8de3ad5df12b434a9a.png)

The region above enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=\sqrt{x}$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=1.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =\sqrt{x} \\ {x}^{2}-\sqrt{x} & =0 \\ \sqrt{x}({x}^{3/2}-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, our limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/7aaa03f21130529bdf5572acac29bfe7566724d8acacc99ca5fc0b035de0398b.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{2}.$

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/a7bd5b7f8e61be991cb6a54e9b1277bd6df4fd874dbd72ec90802b4f957c31bd.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(1)-({x}^{2})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222582/assets/ee93f00e178fa7fd7b8702538298a15a5c98d94205deeb71401a49d8dd891545.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(1)-(\sqrt{x})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-{x}^{2}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[1-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}((1-{x}^{2})^{2}-(1-\sqrt{x})^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}-x+2\sqrt{x})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{1}{5}\,{x}^{5}-\frac{2}{3}\,{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{4}{3}\,{x}^{3/2}\text{ })|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi ((\frac{1}{5}\,(1)^{5}-\frac{2}{3}\,(1)^{3}-\frac{1}{2}\,(1)^{2}+\frac{4}{3}\,(1)^{3/2})-(0)) \\  & =\pi (\frac{11}{30}) \\  & =\frac{11\pi }{30}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

The region above enclosed by the curves y=x2 and y=x is rotated 2π radians about the line y=1. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

a
3π11
b
3π10
c
14π19
d
11π30
e
18π5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation:

x2=xx2−x=0x(x3/2−1)=0x=0,1 Hence, our limits of integration are from x=0 to x=1.

Now, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the inner curve y=x, and

  • leaves through the outer curve y=x2.

Next, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

  • Step I. Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve y=x2.

The corresponding volume is given by Vouter=π∫01[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫01[(1)−(x2)]2dx=π∫01[1−x2]2dx.

  • Step II. Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve y=x.

The corresponding volume is given by Vinner=π∫01[(upper)−(lower)]2dx=π∫01[(1)−(x)]2dx=π∫01[1−x]2dx.

  • Step III. Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as V=Vouter−Vinner=π∫01[1−x2]2dx−π∫01[1−x]2dx=π∫01((1−x2)2−(1−x)2)dx=π∫01(x4−2x2−x+2x)dx=π(15x5−23x3−12x2+43x3/2 )|01=π((15(1)5−23(1)3−12(1)2+43(1)3/2)−(0))=π(1130)=11π30.
